acceleration: The vector rate of change of velocity with time, whose sign indicates the direction in which velocity is changing.
acceleration-time graph: A graph with acceleration on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, where the area under the curve equals the change in velocity.
airspeed: The speed of an aircraft relative to the surrounding mass of air, independent of wind effects.
angular acceleration, α: The rate of change of angular velocity with time, measured in radians per second squared.
angular displacement, δθ: The change in angular position over a time interval, measured in radians, with counterclockwise taken as positive.
angular position, θ: The orientation of a rotating body relative to a reference direction, measured in radians.
angular velocity, ω: The rate at which angle changes during circular motion, equal to 2π/T, measured in radians per second.
arc length, s: The distance a point on a rotating body travels along its curved path, equal to r·θ when θ is in radians.
area under the curve: The region between a graph's curve and the time axis; on a velocity-time graph it equals displacement.
average acceleration: The change in velocity divided by elapsed time, equal to the slope of a secant line on a velocity-time graph.
average quantity: A value computed over a time interval, found from the slope of a secant line or total change divided by total time.
average velocity: Displacement divided by elapsed time, equal to the slope of a secant line on a position-time graph.
axis identification: The crucial first step in graph analysis of explicitly recognizing which physical quantity each axis represents.
centripetal acceleration: The acceleration component that changes the direction of velocity, equal to v²/r and directed toward the center.
centripetal acceleration, a_c: The acceleration directed toward the center of a circular path, equal to v²/r, constantly changing the direction of velocity.
change in velocity: The difference between final and initial velocity, equal to the signed area under an acceleration-time graph.
closing speed: The rate at which the gap between two objects shrinks, equal to the magnitude of their relative velocity along the line joining them.
complementary angles: Two angles that sum to 90 degrees, which produce the same range when projectiles are launched at the same initial speed on level ground.
concave down: A curve that bends downward, indicating a decreasing slope and therefore a negative acceleration.
concave up: A curve that bends upward like a cup, indicating an increasing slope and therefore a positive acceleration.
concavity: The directional curvature of a graph, with concave up indicating increasing slope and concave down decreasing slope.
constant acceleration: Motion in which the rate of change of velocity is the same at every instant, giving a linear velocity-time relationship.
constant angular acceleration: A condition in which α does not change throughout the motion, allowing the standard rotational kinematics equations to be used.
critical point: A location on a graph where the slope is zero or undefined, corresponding to a maximum, minimum, or inflection point.
crossing time: The time required to cross a river or similar obstacle, determined by the velocity component perpendicular to the current.
curved graph: A graph that bends, indicating that the rate of change of the vertical quantity with respect to the horizontal quantity varies.
derivative relationship: The mathematical link in which velocity is the time derivative of position and acceleration is the time derivative of velocity.
direct proportionality: A relationship in which one quantity is a constant multiple of another, as when linear speed is proportional to radius at constant angular velocity.
displacement: The vector difference between final and initial position, calculated as Δx = x_final − x_initial.
distance: The scalar total of all path lengths an object travels, accumulated regardless of direction and always non-negative.
distance traveled: The total length of the path an object covers, equal to the sum of the absolute areas under a velocity-time graph.
drift: Lateral displacement from the intended path caused by the motion of a medium such as a crosscurrent or crosswind.
final velocity: The velocity of an object at the end of the analyzed time interval, denoted v and measured in m/s.
free fall: Motion in which gravity is the only force acting, producing a constant acceleration of 9.8 m/s² toward Earth's center.
frequency, f: The number of complete revolutions per second, equal to 1/T and measured in hertz.
graph translation: The process of transferring information from one type of motion graph to another using slope and area relationships.
gravitational acceleration: The acceleration of objects near Earth's surface due to gravity, equal to 9.8 m/s² toward Earth's center.
ground frame: A reference frame attached to a stationary observer on Earth's surface, the default frame for most kinematics problems.
ground velocity: The velocity of an object as observed from a stationary position on the ground, including all effects of a moving medium.
heading: The direction an object points or aims, which can differ from its actual path when moving through a moving medium.
horizontal component: The part of a projectile's velocity or displacement parallel to the ground, which stays constant because no horizontal force acts.
horizontal launch: A projectile situation in which the initial velocity is entirely horizontal with zero vertical component.
independence principle: The idea that the horizontal and vertical components of projectile motion are fully independent, linked only by time.
inertial reference frame: A reference frame moving at constant velocity with zero acceleration, in which Newton's laws apply in standard form without fictitious forces.
initial angular velocity, ω₀: The angular velocity at the start of the analyzed time interval, often zero when an object starts from rest.
initial conditions: The starting values of position and velocity needed to fully determine motion, since area gives change rather than absolute value.
initial speed: The magnitude of the initial velocity vector, denoted v₀, indicating how fast a projectile moves at launch regardless of direction.
initial velocity: The velocity of an object at the start of the analyzed time interval, denoted v₀ and measured in m/s.
instantaneous acceleration: The acceleration at a single instant, equal to the slope of the tangent line to a velocity-time curve at that point.
instantaneous quantity: A value defined at a single instant, found from the slope of a tangent line rather than a secant line.
instantaneous velocity: The velocity at a single instant, equal to the slope of the tangent line to a position-time curve at that point.
invariance: The property that certain quantities, such as the relative velocity between two objects, have the same value in any inertial frame.
kinematic equations: Four algebraic relations linking position, velocity, acceleration, and time, applicable exclusively to constant-acceleration motion.
launch angle: The angle between the initial velocity vector and the horizontal, which sets the ratio of horizontal to vertical velocity components.
linear graph: A graph that forms a straight line, indicating a constant rate of change of the vertical quantity with respect to the horizontal quantity.
linear speed, v: The distance traveled per unit time along a circular path, related to angular speed by v = ωr and measured in m/s.
maximum height: The highest vertical position a projectile reaches, occurring when vertical velocity is zero, equal to v₀ᵧ²/(2g) for level launch.
multi stage motion: Motion made of distinct segments with different constant accelerations, each analyzed separately while keeping velocity continuous at transitions.
multi-representation problem: A problem requiring simultaneous analysis of two or more different graph representations of the same motion.
non-uniform acceleration: Acceleration that changes with time, appearing as curvature rather than a straight line on a velocity-time graph.
nonuniform circular motion: Circular motion in which angular velocity changes with time, requiring both tangential and centripetal acceleration to describe it.
parabolic path: The geometric shape of a projectile's trajectory, produced by constant horizontal velocity combined with constant vertical acceleration.
peak of trajectory: The instant when a projectile's vertical velocity is zero, occurring at maximum height while acceleration remains 9.8 m/s² downward.
period, t: The time required for an object in circular motion to complete one full revolution, measured in seconds.
position: A vector quantity describing an object's location along a coordinate axis relative to a chosen origin.
position-time graph: A graph with position on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, where the slope at any point equals velocity.
projectile motion: The curved path followed by an object moving under gravity alone, with constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration.
quadratic equation: A second-degree polynomial equation arising when solving for flight time when launch and landing heights differ.
quadratic solutions: The two possible values of time or position from a quadratic kinematics equation, requiring physical interpretation to select the valid one.
radial direction: The direction pointing straight toward or away from the center of a circle, along which centripetal acceleration acts.
radian: A unit of angle measure in which one full revolution equals 2π radians, defined as the ratio of arc length to radius.
radius, r: The distance from the center of a circular path to the point of interest, which sets the linear speed for a given angular velocity.
range: The horizontal distance a projectile travels from launch to landing, equal to horizontal velocity times time of flight.
rate of change: The mathematical concept underlying slope interpretation, indicating how fast the vertical quantity changes relative to the horizontal quantity.
reasonableness check: Evaluating a calculated answer against physical expectations, including proper sign, plausible magnitude, and correct units.
reference frame: A coordinate system attached to a particular observer in which all position and velocity measurements are made.
relative velocity: The velocity of an object measured by an observer in a particular frame, found by vectorially subtracting the observer's velocity.
resultant velocity: A single velocity vector equal to the vector sum of several velocities, representing the net motion in a given frame.
rigid body rotation: The rotation of a body in which all points keep fixed positions relative to each other and share the same angular velocity.
scalar: A quantity fully specified by magnitude alone with no direction, such as mass, time, speed, or distance.
scaling: A mathematical relationship describing how one quantity changes when another is multiplied by some factor.
secant line: A straight line crossing a curve at two points, whose slope equals the average rate of change between those points.
sign consistency: The practice of keeping the same direction convention for all vectors throughout a problem so signs correctly indicate direction.
sign convention: The consistent assignment of positive and negative signs to directions, maintained throughout a problem for correct vector treatment.
signed area: An area calculation that accounts for whether the curve lies above or below the axis, essential for finding net displacement on a v-t graph.
slope: The steepness of a line or curve at a point, representing the rate of change of the vertical quantity and calculated as rise over run.
slowing down: The state in which an object's speed decreases over time, occurring when velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.
speed: The scalar magnitude of velocity, indicating how fast an object moves regardless of direction and always non-negative.
speeding up: The state in which an object's speed increases over time, occurring when velocity and acceleration have the same sign.
subscript chain: The ordering of subscripts in velocity addition where inner letters match and cancel, leaving only the outermost frames related.
subscript notation: A convention in which v with subscript AB denotes the velocity of A as measured by B, used to track frames in velocity addition.
tangent line: A straight line touching a curve at exactly one point and matching its slope there, used to find an instantaneous rate of change.
tangential acceleration: The acceleration component that changes the speed of a point on a rotating body, equal to αr and directed along the velocity.
tangential direction: The direction along the circle at any point, perpendicular to the radius and along the velocity vector.
terminal velocity: The constant speed reached when air resistance equals gravity, neglected in ideal projectile motion but significant over large falls.
time interval: The duration of motion being analyzed, throughout which all kinematic conditions including constant acceleration must hold.
time of flight: The total time a projectile stays in the air from launch to landing, determined entirely by the vertical motion.
total acceleration: The vector sum of tangential and centripetal acceleration, with magnitude equal to the square root of the sum of their squares.
trajectory: The curved path a projectile follows through space, which is a parabola in ideal projectile motion.
turning point: A point where an object reverses direction, characterized by zero velocity and nonzero acceleration.
uniform circular motion: Motion in a circle at constant speed, where velocity magnitude is constant but direction continually changes and acceleration is purely centripetal.
variable acceleration: Motion in which the rate of change of velocity differs at different instants, invalidating the kinematics equations.
variable identification method: A systematic approach to kinematics problems that lists and classifies all five variables before selecting an equation.
vector: A quantity requiring both magnitude and direction for full specification, such as position, displacement, velocity, or acceleration.
vector addition: The process of combining velocity vectors by adding their components, needed when velocities point in different directions.
vector decomposition: The mathematical process of splitting a vector into perpendicular components, usually horizontal and vertical, using trigonometry.
velocity: The vector rate of change of position with time, whose sign indicates direction and whose magnitude is speed.
velocity addition formula: The equation v_AC = v_AB + v_BC, stating that velocities add vectorially across frames when intermediate subscripts match.
velocity-time graph: A graph with velocity on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, where slope equals acceleration and area equals displacement.
vertical component: The part of a projectile's velocity or displacement perpendicular to the ground, which changes due to gravity at 9.8 m/s² downward.
water frame: A reference frame moving with the river current, in which the water appears at rest and the banks appear to move upstream.
zero crossing: A point where a graph crosses the horizontal axis, indicating that the plotted quantity is zero at that instant.
action at a distance: A force acting between objects without physical contact, with gravity being the prime example in AP Physics 1.
angle of repose: The angle at which an object on an inclined surface begins to slide, determined solely by the coefficient of static friction.
apparent weight: The normal force an object feels, which differs from true weight during acceleration, equal to mg + ma when accelerating upward.
atwood machine: A system of two masses connected by a rope over a pulley, used to study the dynamics of connected objects.
banking angle: The angle by which a roadway is tilted inward from horizontal, allowing the normal force to contribute to the centripetal force.
bound orbit: An orbital state with negative total mechanical energy, meaning the satellite lacks enough energy to escape to infinity.
center of mass: The point at which an object's mass is effectively concentrated for gravitational purposes, where the weight force acts in torque calculations.
center to center distance: The distance r in the gravitation equation, measured from the center of one mass to the center of the other, not from surfaces.
centripetal force: The net force directed toward the center of a circular path, equal to mv²/r and supplied by real forces such as tension, gravity, or friction.
coefficient of kinetic friction: The dimensionless quantity μk giving the ratio of kinetic friction to normal force, always less than the corresponding static coefficient.
coefficient of static friction: The dimensionless quantity μₛ giving the ratio of maximum static friction to normal force, set by surface roughness and materials.
component along the ramp: The component of gravity parallel to an incline, equal to mg·sinθ, which causes acceleration along the slope.
component form: The expression of Newton's second law as separate equations for each perpendicular direction: ∑Fx = max, ∑Fy = may.
component perpendicular to ramp: The component of gravity perpendicular to an incline, equal to mg·cosθ, which is balanced by the normal force.
connected objects: Two or more objects linked by a rope, string, or direct contact so that their motions are constrained to be related.
conservation of mechanical energy: The principle that total mechanical energy stays constant when only conservative forces do work.
constraint: A condition relating the motions of different objects, such as equal acceleration magnitudes for objects joined by a rope.
constraint equation: An extra equation relating the accelerations of connected objects based on their physical link, such as equal acceleration magnitudes.
contact force: A force requiring physical contact between objects, such as normal force, friction, tension, or an applied push or pull.
contact patch: The region where two surfaces physically touch, where friction acts and relative motion or its tendency must be assessed.
critical angle: The maximum incline angle at which an object can remain at rest, equal to arctan(μₛ), also called the angle of repose.
design speed: The speed for which a banked curve is optimized, at which the horizontal component of the normal force alone provides the needed centripetal force.
dimensional analysis: A verification technique checking that all terms in an equation share the same units, used to catch setup errors before solving.
direction convention: A consistent choice of which direction is positive, maintained for all objects in a connected system to avoid sign errors.
dissipation: The conversion of mechanical energy into thermal energy through friction, reducing the energy available to do work.
effective spring constant: The single spring-constant value that would give the same force-displacement relationship as a combination of springs.
elastic potential energy: Energy stored in a deformed spring, calculated as ½kx², always non-negative and depending only on the magnitude of displacement.
energy transformation: The conversion of energy from one form to another, as between elastic potential energy and kinetic energy in a spring system.
equilibrium: A state in which the net force on an object is zero and its acceleration is zero, either at rest or moving at constant velocity.
equilibrium position: The position where a spring exerts zero force, corresponding to its natural unstretched length, the reference for all displacements.
escape speed: The minimum initial speed needed to reach infinite distance from a gravitating body, equal to √(2GM/r), where total mechanical energy is zero.
external force: A force exerted on a system by an object outside it; only external forces can change a system's momentum or cause acceleration.
force decomposition: The process of splitting a force vector into perpendicular components, usually horizontal and vertical or parallel and perpendicular to a surface.
free body diagram: A drawing that isolates one object and represents every force acting on it as an arrow showing magnitude and direction.
friction transition: The sudden change from static to kinetic friction when an object begins to slide, with friction dropping from μₛN to μkN.
geosynchronous orbit: A circular orbit whose period equals the planet's rotation period, occurring at a specific radius given by T = 2π√(r³/GM).
gravitational field strength, g: The gravitational force per unit mass at a location, calculated as g = GM/r², varying with distance from the source.
gravitational force: The attractive force between two masses; near Earth's surface it equals an object's mass times the field strength g.
gravitational potential energy: Energy stored in the gravitational field between two masses, calculated as PE = −GMm/r, approaching zero at infinite separation.
gravitational potential well: A conceptual model showing that gravitational potential energy decreases (becomes more negative) as an object approaches a massive body.
hooke's law: The principle that a spring's force is proportional and opposite to displacement from equilibrium, expressed as F = −kx.
ideal banking angle: The specific banking angle at which a vehicle can round a curve at a given speed without friction, given by θ = arctan(v²/rg).
ideal pulley: A pulley with zero mass and no axle friction, which changes only the direction of tension, not its magnitude.
impending motion: The state just before an object begins to slide, when static friction has reached its maximum value μₛN.
inertia: The property quantifying an object's resistance to changes in its motion, proportional to mass and not itself a force.
inside loop: A vertical circular path along an inner surface, where the normal force points toward the center at all positions.
interaction pair: Two equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces arising from a single interaction, acting on different objects per Newton's third law.
internal force: A force one part of a system exerts on another part of the same system, which does not contribute to the net external force.
inverse square law: The relationship that gravity decreases in proportion to the square of distance, because it spreads over a sphere whose area grows as r².
isolated object analysis: Applying Newton's second law to a single object within a larger system, using the system acceleration to find unknown forces like tension.
kinematic constraint: A physical restriction linking the motions of connected objects, such as equal acceleration magnitudes for objects joined by an inextensible rope.
kinetic friction: The friction force opposing motion when surfaces slide against each other, with magnitude equal to the kinetic coefficient times the normal force.
lever arm: The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of a force, representing the effective moment arm that sets torque magnitude.
line of action: The line extending infinitely along a force vector's direction, used to find the perpendicular distance defining the lever arm.
mass independence of orbital speed: The principle that orbital speed depends only on the central mass and orbital radius, not on the orbiting object's mass.
massless rope: An idealized rope of zero mass that transmits tension uniformly along its length, since no net force is needed to accelerate any part of it.
minimum speed: The lowest speed at which an object can maintain contact at the top of a vertical loop, occurring when the normal force is zero, given by v = √(gr).
modified atwood machine: A variation of the classic Atwood setup in which one or more masses move along a horizontal or inclined surface rather than hanging vertically.
moment arm: Another name for the lever arm, emphasizing its role in producing a rotational moment, or torque, about a chosen axis.
net force: The vector sum of all forces acting on an object; when it is zero the object is in equilibrium and does not accelerate.
newton meter: The SI unit of torque, representing the rotational effect of one newton applied perpendicular to a one-meter moment arm.
newton's first law: An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion continues at constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force.
newton's third law: When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A; these forces are of the same type and act on different objects.
normal force: The contact force perpendicular to a surface that prevents objects from passing through each other, arising from electromagnetic interactions.
orbital period: The time to complete one orbit, calculated as T = 2π√(r³/GM), increasing with the 3/2 power of the orbital radius.
orbital speed: The tangential speed needed to maintain a circular orbit of radius r, calculated as v = √(GM/r), decreasing as radius increases.
orbital transfer: A maneuver that changes a satellite's orbit by adding or removing kinetic energy to raise or lower the orbital radius.
parallel spring combination: An arrangement where springs share the same displacement, giving an effective spring constant equal to the sum of the individual constants.
perpendicular component: The part of a force acting at a right angle to the line from the pivot to the application point, calculated as F times sinθ.
pivot point: The fixed location about which an object rotates, also called the fulcrum or axis, from which lever-arm distances are measured.
potential energy well: A graph of potential energy as a function of position; for a spring its parabolic minimum at equilibrium indicates a restoring force.
ramp decomposition: The process of resolving gravity into components parallel and perpendicular to an incline, mg·sinθ and mg·cosθ respectively.
reactive force: A force whose magnitude is set by other forces in the system rather than by an intrinsic property, adjusting to maintain equilibrium up to a limit.
relative motion: The motion of one object as seen from the reference frame of another object in contact, which determines the direction of kinetic friction.
restoring force: A force that always acts to return a system to its equilibrium position, opposing displacement as a spring does.
rotated coordinate system: A coordinate system with axes aligned parallel and perpendicular to an incline rather than horizontal and vertical.
rotational equilibrium: A state in which the net torque on an object is zero, so its angular acceleration is zero and it does not rotate or rotates at constant angular velocity.
series spring combination: An arrangement where springs share the same force transmitted through a chain, giving an effective constant softer than any single spring.
spring constant: A measure of spring stiffness in newtons per meter, equal to the force needed to produce one meter of displacement; larger k means a stiffer spring.
static equilibrium: A state in which both net force and net torque are zero, so an object is at rest with no tendency to translate or rotate.
static friction: The friction force preventing relative sliding between surfaces in contact, adjusting its magnitude up to a maximum to match the applied force.
strategic pivot: A pivot chosen at the location of an unknown force to eliminate that force from the torque equation and simplify the solution.
surface gravity: The gravitational field strength at a planet's surface, calculated as g = GM/R², depending on both the planet's mass and radius.
system: A collection of objects analyzed together as a single entity, in which internal forces cancel and only external forces determine acceleration.
system equation: Newton's second law applied to all connected objects as one unit, with the net external force equal to total system mass times acceleration.
system isolation: An analysis technique that considers one object at a time and includes only the forces acting on that specific object.
tangential velocity: The instantaneous velocity of an object in circular motion, always directed tangent to the circular path and perpendicular to the radius.
tendency of motion: The direction an object would move relative to a surface in the absence of friction, which determines the direction of static friction.
tension: The pulling force transmitted through a connector such as a rope, string, or cable, pulling equally on the two objects it joins.
third law pair: Two forces satisfying Newton's third law: equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, of the same type, and acting on two different objects.
torque: The rotational analog of force, calculated as the product of the lever arm and the perpendicular force component, causing angular acceleration if unbalanced.
total mechanical energy: The sum of an orbiting object's kinetic and gravitational potential energy; negative indicates a bound orbit, zero the escape threshold.
uniform object: An object with constant density throughout its volume, so its center of mass coincides with its geometric center.
uniform tension: The condition in which tension has the same value at every point in a rope, occurring when the rope is massless and the pulley frictionless.
universal gravitational constant, g: The proportionality constant in Newton's law of gravitation, equal to 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², quantifying gravitational attraction between any two masses.
vector sum: The result of adding vectors by combining their components; for forces, the vector sum of all forces gives the net force.
verification step: The process of validating a solution by recomputing an unknown force using objects independently and checking that the values agree.
vertical spring equilibrium: The position where a mass hanging from a vertical spring rests, where the spring force k times the stretch equals the weight mg.
weight: The gravitational force on an object, equal to mg and directed toward Earth's center.
weight component: The part of the gravitational force acting in a specific direction, mg·sinθ parallel to an incline and mg·cosθ perpendicular to it.
work-energy relationship: The principle that the work done on a spring equals the change in its elastic potential energy.
amplitude: The maximum displacement from equilibrium in simple harmonic motion, the point where all energy is potential and speed is zero.
angular velocity: The rate at which an object rotates, measured in radians per second and denoted ω, the rotational analog of linear velocity.
average power: Total work divided by the total time interval, representing the average rate of energy transfer over a specified period.
change in potential energy: The quantity ΔPE = mg·Δh, independent of the choice of reference height; only the change in PE has physical meaning.
combination strategy: A solving approach that uses energy conservation to find speed at a point, then applies Newton's second law there to find force.
complete energy equation for rolling: The equation mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω², which accounts for both translational and rotational kinetic energy of a rolling object descending height h.
component of force: The projection of a force vector along a specified direction, calculated with trigonometry such as F cos(θ) parallel to displacement.
conservation of energy: The principle that the total energy of an isolated system stays constant, with energy only transformed between forms, never created or destroyed.
conservative force: A force whose work depends only on initial and final positions, not the path; gravity and spring forces are conservative.
constant velocity condition: A state of motion with unchanging speed and direction, requiring zero net force so applied and resistive forces balance.
critical speed: The minimum speed at which an object maintains contact with a track at a point in circular motion, occurring when the normal force is zero.
delta ke: The change in kinetic energy, defined as KE_final − KE_initial, equal to the net work done and possibly positive, negative, or zero.
derivation from f equals ma: The process of proving W_net = ΔKE by multiplying Newton's second law by displacement and converting ma·d to ΔKE with kinematics.
efficiency: The ratio of useful power output to total power input, expressed as a fraction or percentage of input energy serving the intended function.
energy bar chart: A visual representation showing bars for each energy form at initial and final states, used to track energy transformations systematically.
energy dissipation: The conversion of mechanical energy to thermal energy through nonconservative forces such as friction, conserving total energy.
energy distribution in rolling: The split of a rolling object's total kinetic energy between translational and rotational forms, set by its moment of inertia coefficient.
energy methods: A solving approach using energy conservation or the work-energy theorem to relate initial and final states without tracking the detailed path.
energy transfer: The process by which work done on an object increases or decreases its energy, with positive work adding and negative work removing energy.
energy transfer at boundaries: The principle that the kinetic energy at the end of one segment equals the kinetic energy at the start of the next, linking sequential calculations.
force component parallel to displacement: The part of a force vector lying along the direction of motion, calculated as F cos(θ), which determines the work that force does.
force methods: A solving approach that analyzes forces and acceleration at a specific instant using Newton's second law, requiring free body diagrams.
frequency: The number of complete oscillations per unit time, equal to the reciprocal of the period and measured in hertz.
friction work: The work done by kinetic friction, always negative because friction opposes the sliding motion, calculated as −f·d.
gravitational to kinetic conversion: The process by which an object descending in a gravitational field gains kinetic energy as gravity does positive work increasing KE by mgh.
instantaneous power: The power delivered or consumed at a specific instant, calculated as the product of force and velocity at that moment.
joule: The SI unit of work and energy, equal to one newton of force applied over one meter of displacement when force and displacement are parallel.
kinetic energy: The energy an object has due to its motion, calculated as KE = ½mv², where m is mass and v is speed.
kinetic friction work: The work done by kinetic friction on a sliding object, calculated as −μk·N·d, representing mechanical energy converted to thermal energy.
kinetic to thermal conversion: The process by which kinetic energy decreases due to friction work, with the negative work representing energy becoming thermal energy in the surface.
linear relationship: A mathematical relationship in which doubling one variable exactly doubles the dependent variable, as in P = Fv at constant force.
linear restoring force: A force proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always directed toward it, the defining feature of simple harmonic motion.
mass distribution: The spatial arrangement of mass within an object relative to a rotation axis; mass farther from the axis gives a larger moment of inertia.
mass flow rate: The mass of material passing a point per unit time, often dm/dt, used to compute power in fluid systems with continuous throughput.
maximum velocity: The speed of an oscillating mass as it passes equilibrium, calculated as v_max = A√(k/m), where all energy is kinetic.
mechanical energy: The sum of a system's kinetic and potential energy: E_mech = KE + PE, conserved when only conservative forces do work.
moment of inertia: The rotational analog of mass, representing resistance to angular acceleration, equal to the sum of each mass element times its distance from the axis squared.
moment of inertia coefficient: The dimensionless factor c in I = c·mr² for a standard shape, determining what fraction of total kinetic energy becomes rotational when rolling.
multi-segment problem: A physics problem in which an object passes through two or more regions of different force, each treated with the work-energy theorem separately.
multi-stage efficiency: The overall efficiency of a system with several energy-conversion stages, found by multiplying all the individual stage efficiencies.
negative work: Work done when the force component parallel to displacement points opposite to the displacement, removing energy from the system.
net work: The algebraic sum of the work done by all forces acting on an object, with positive and negative contributions added by sign.
no slip condition: The requirement that there be no relative motion at the contact point between a rolling object and surface, maintained by static friction.
non-conservative force: A force whose work depends on the path taken, not just the endpoints; friction and air resistance are examples with no defined potential energy.
nonconservative force: A force such as friction or air resistance whose work depends on the path, causing mechanical energy to dissipate into other forms.
path independence: The property of conservative forces that the work between two points is the same regardless of path, allowing potential energy to be defined.
period: The time required for one complete oscillation cycle, given by T = 2π√(m/k) for a mass on a spring.
perpendicular force: A force acting at 90° to the displacement, which does zero work because cos(90°) = 0 regardless of force or distance.
point mass moment of inertia: The moment of inertia of a point mass m at distance r from the axis, simply I = mr², the building block for extended objects.
position dependent velocity: The relationship v = √(k/m)·√(A² − x²), showing how speed varies nonlinearly with displacement during oscillation.
positive work: Work done when the force component parallel to displacement points in the same direction as the displacement, adding energy to the system.
power: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, calculated as work divided by time and measured in watts.
proportional reasoning: A problem-solving strategy that compares ratios of quantities between scenarios without calculating absolute values.
quadratic dependence: The relationship in which elastic potential energy is proportional to displacement squared, so doubling compression quadruples stored energy.
rate quantity: A physical quantity defined as the ratio of a measurement to a time interval, with shorter intervals giving larger rate values.
reference level: The position where gravitational potential energy is defined as zero; the choice is arbitrary, usually set at the lowest point to simplify calculations.
resistive force: Any force opposing motion that dissipates mechanical energy into thermal energy, including friction, air resistance, and drag.
rolling acceleration: The linear acceleration of an object rolling down an incline, given by a = g·sin(θ)/(1+c), smaller for larger moment-of-inertia coefficients.
rolling without slipping: Motion where the contact point of a rolling object has zero instantaneous velocity relative to the surface, requiring v = rω.
rotational inertia coefficient: The numerical factor in a standard shape's moment-of-inertia formula, such as ½ for a solid cylinder, indicating how far mass is distributed from the axis.
rotational kinetic energy: The kinetic energy an object has due to rotation about an axis, calculated as ½Iω², added to translational KE for a rolling object.
scalar addition of work: The process of summing work contributions from several forces by ordinary signed addition rather than vector addition, since work is scalar.
scalar quantity: A physical quantity with magnitude but no direction, such as energy, mass, speed, or temperature, which can be added directly.
simple pendulum: An idealized oscillator of a point mass on a massless string that exhibits simple harmonic motion at small angles with period T = 2π√(L/g).
small angle approximation: The simplification that sin(θ) is approximately θ in radians for angles below about 15 degrees, needed for true simple harmonic pendulum motion.
state: A complete description of a system at one instant, including position, velocity, and configuration, used as an initial or final condition.
system boundary: An imaginary surface defining what is inside and outside a system, used to track energy entering as input power and leaving as output or waste heat.
thermal energy: Internal energy associated with random molecular motion, which mechanical energy converts into when friction acts.
total energy: The sum of all energy forms in a system including mechanical and thermal energy, always conserved per the first law of thermodynamics.
variable force: A force whose magnitude or direction changes with position, time, or velocity, invalidating constant-acceleration kinematics and often requiring energy methods.
variable force work: Work done by a force whose magnitude or direction changes during displacement, sometimes found from energy conservation without instant-by-instant calculation.
vector angle: The geometric angle between two vectors, measured from one to the other, which determines the cosine factor in a work calculation.
watt: The SI unit of power equal to one joule per second, representing the rate at which one joule of energy is transferred or converted each second.
work: Energy transferred to or from an object by a force acting through a displacement, calculated as W = Fd cos(θ).
work against gravity: Energy transferred to an object when an external force lifts it against gravity, stored as gravitational potential energy.
work by a force: Energy transferred by a single force, calculated as Fd cos(θ); positive work increases kinetic energy and negative work decreases it.
work by gravity: The work done by gravity, equal to mgh where h is the vertical displacement; negative when an object rises and positive when it falls.
work by non-conservative forces: The quantity W_nc = ΔKE + ΔPE = ΔE_mech; when negative, mechanical energy decreases as energy is transferred to thermal form.
work-energy theorem: The fundamental principle that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ½mv² − ½mv₀².
acoustic energy: Energy carried away by sound waves radiated in a collision, representing mechanical energy that propagates outward into the surrounding medium.
angular momentum: The rotational analog of linear momentum, calculated as L = mvr for a point mass or L = Iω for a rigid body.
aphelion: The point in an elliptical orbit farthest from the central body, where orbital speed is minimum due to conservation of angular momentum.
arctangent relationship: The trigonometric function giving a vector's angle from its components, calculated as the inverse tangent of the y component divided by the x component.
areal velocity: The rate at which the line from the central body to an orbiting object sweeps out area, equal to L/2m and constant when angular momentum is conserved.
average force: The constant force that would produce the same impulse over a given time interval as an actual varying force, calculated as F_avg = Δp/Δt.
center of mass reference frame: A frame moving with the center of mass, in which the total system momentum is always zero and collisions appear symmetric.
center of mass velocity: The velocity at which the center of mass moves, equal to total momentum divided by total mass, constant when the net external force is zero.
central force: A force directed along the line joining two bodies, exerting zero torque about the center and thereby conserving angular momentum.
closed system: A system with no net external force acting on it, ensuring that the system's total momentum stays constant by the impulse-momentum theorem.
coefficient of restitution, e: A dimensionless quantity equal to the ratio of separation speed to approach speed, ranging from 0 for perfectly inelastic to 1 for perfectly elastic collisions.
collision: An interaction in which objects exert large forces on each other over a short time, with collision forces being internal to the system of colliding objects.
collision classification: Categorizing collisions as elastic, inelastic, or perfectly inelastic based on whether kinetic energy is conserved and whether objects stick together.
collision forces: The contact forces between colliding objects, appearing as Newton's third law pairs and internal to a system containing both objects.
collision time: The duration Δt during which colliding objects remain in contact, inversely related to the average force for a given momentum change.
component decomposition: The process of splitting a vector quantity into perpendicular parts using trigonometry based on the angle with the reference axes.
component independence: The principle that momentum is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction, since a force component in one direction cannot affect momentum in the perpendicular one.
conservation of angular momentum: The principle that total angular momentum stays constant when the net external torque is zero, expressed as I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.
coordinate system: A chosen orientation of perpendicular axes that determines the sign and direction assignment for all velocity and momentum components in a problem.
crumple zone: A region of a vehicle designed to deform on impact, increasing the stopping time and thereby reducing the peak force on occupants.
deflection angle: The angle between an object's final velocity vector and the reference axis, found as the arctangent of perpendicular over parallel velocity components.
deformation energy: Energy stored in the changed arrangement of a material after permanent deformation, representing work done against internal molecular forces.
direction reversal: A change of motion in which an object's velocity switches from positive to negative or vice versa, producing a larger momentum change than merely stopping.
discrete mass system: A collection of point particles with definite masses at specific locations, contrasted with a continuous mass distribution such as a rod or disk.
elastic collision: A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, with objects bouncing apart without converting energy to heat or deformation.
energy transformation pathway: The specific mechanism by which kinetic energy converts to other forms during a collision, such as permanent deformation, heat, sound, or internal vibration.
entropy: A thermodynamic quantity measuring a system's disorder, which increases when ordered kinetic energy converts to disordered thermal energy, making a process irreversible.
exhaust velocity: The speed at which combustion products leave a rocket nozzle; higher exhaust velocity transfers more momentum per unit mass of fuel, making the rocket more efficient.
explosion: An interaction in which a single object or group separates into pieces due to internal forces, leaving the center-of-mass velocity unchanged.
external torque: A torque applied to a system by an object or force outside it, which can change the system's angular momentum.
follow-through: Continuing motion after contact in a throwing or striking action, ensuring maximum speed at the moment of contact to maximize the impulse delivered.
force-time graph: A graph with force on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, where the area under the curve represents the impulse delivered.
glancing collision: A collision in which objects strike off-center and deflect at an angle, producing final velocities with components in multiple perpendicular directions.
impulse: The product of force and the time interval over which it acts, J = F·Δt, representing the total effect of a force in changing momentum.
impulse-momentum theorem: The statement that impulse equals the change in momentum, J = Δp, derived directly from Newton's second law multiplied by a time interval.
inelastic collision: A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not, with some kinetic energy converted to heat, sound, or deformation.
inelastic rotational collision: A collision in which rotating objects stick together, conserving angular momentum but losing kinetic energy to friction or deformation.
internal explosion: A process in which objects within a system separate due to forces between them; being internal, these forces do not change total momentum or center-of-mass velocity.
internal forces: Forces between objects within a defined system, appearing as Newton's third law pairs that cancel when summed over the whole system.
internal motion: The motion of individual particles within a system relative to one another, which can change individual velocities but not the center-of-mass velocity.
internal torque: A torque between components within a defined system, which redistributes angular momentum among the parts but cannot change the total.
kepler's second law: The statement that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, following from conservation of angular momentum in central-force motion.
linear momentum: The product of an object's mass and velocity, p = mv, a vector quantity representing the amount and direction of motion at an instant.
mass-weighted average: An averaging method that multiplies each value by its corresponding mass before summing, giving heavier objects proportionally greater influence.
mechanically reversible: A process that can proceed in either direction without violating physical laws, characteristic of a perfectly elastic collision that does not increase entropy.
momentum conservation equation: The mathematical statement that total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after, written m1v1i + m2v2i = m1v1f + m2v2f for two bodies.
negligible external impulse: When external forces act for so short a time that their impulse is small compared to internal impulses, momentum conservation holds approximately.
net external force: The vector sum of all forces on a system from sources outside its boundary; when this sum is zero, total system momentum stays constant.
net impulse: The total impulse accounting for direction, calculated as the algebraic sum of positive and negative areas under a force-time graph.
newton's second law for systems: The equation F_net,ext = M_total × a_cm, stating that only external forces determine the center-of-mass acceleration.
non conservative force: A force that converts mechanical energy to other forms such as heat, or adds mechanical energy from another source such as muscle chemical energy.
nonconservative forces: Forces such as friction or air resistance that convert mechanical energy to thermal energy, with work that depends on the path and reduces mechanical energy.
parabolic trajectory: The curved path followed by an object under constant gravitational acceleration without air resistance, which the center of mass of an exploding projectile continues to follow.
peak force: The maximum force reached during an interaction, which alone does not determine impulse because the time of action also matters.
perfectly inelastic collision: A collision in which objects stick together afterward, losing the maximum kinetic energy consistent with momentum conservation.
perihelion: The point in an elliptical orbit closest to the central body, where orbital speed is maximum due to conservation of angular momentum.
potential energy conversion: The process by which energy stored in chemical bonds, a compressed spring, or other configurations becomes kinetic energy during an explosion.
pythagorean combination: Finding a vector's magnitude from its perpendicular components by taking the square root of the sum of their squares.
reaction mass: Material a rocket expels to produce thrust; the rocket must carry this mass to gain momentum, a fundamental limit on rocket performance.
recoil: The backward motion of one object caused by the forward motion of another in an explosion, with the recoiling object gaining equal and opposite momentum.
relative velocity of approach: The speed at which two objects close the distance before a collision, equal to the absolute difference of their initial velocities along the line of impact.
relative velocity of separation: The speed at which two objects move apart after a collision, equal to the absolute difference of their final velocities along the line of impact.
right hand rule: A convention for determining the direction of angular momentum: curl the fingers in the direction of rotation and the thumb points along the vector.
rocket propulsion: A method by which a rocket accelerates by ejecting exhaust mass backward at high speed; by momentum conservation, no external surface is needed to push against.
state quantity: A property such as position, velocity, or momentum that describes a system at one specific instant, contrasted with a process quantity like work or impulse.
system of equations: Two or more equations sharing common unknowns that must be solved simultaneously by substitution or elimination.
total momentum: The sum of all individual momenta in a system, equal to M_total × v_cm, conserved when no net external force acts.
vector magnitude: The length of a vector, representing its size independent of direction, calculated as the hypotenuse of a right triangle from its components.
vector quantity: A physical quantity having both magnitude and direction, requiring sign conventions or component analysis to handle mathematically.
algebraic sum of angular momenta: When combining angular momenta, direction matters; momenta of opposite rotation have opposite signs and partly cancel when summed.
angular acceleration: The rate of change of angular velocity with time, measured in radians per second squared, produced by a net torque per Στ = Iα.
angular displacement: The angle through which an object rotates, measured in radians for consistency in all work and energy calculations.
angular impulse: The product of torque and the time interval over which it acts, equal to the change in angular momentum: J_angular = τΔt = ΔL.
angular momentum conservation: When there is no external torque, a system's total angular momentum stays constant, expressed as I_i·ω_i = I_f·ω_f when the moment of inertia changes.
angular momentum of extended objects: The product of moment of inertia and angular velocity, L = Iω, replacing L = mvr when mass is distributed over a range of radii.
angular momentum vector: The vector quantity L equal to I × ω, directed along the rotation axis by the right-hand rule, with magnitude equal to rotational inertia times rotation rate.
axis shift distance d: The perpendicular distance between the center-of-mass axis and a new parallel axis about which an object actually rotates, entering the parallel axis theorem as Md².
center of gravity: The point at which gravity can be taken to act for torque calculations, coinciding with the center of mass in a uniform gravitational field.
center of mass axis: Any rotation axis passing through an object's center of mass; the moment of inertia is minimized when the axis passes through the center of mass.
combined kinetic energy: The total kinetic energy of a rolling object, equal to the sum of translational KE ½mv² and rotational KE ½Iω².
combined system analysis: A solving approach treating stuck-together or co-moving objects as one system, with final moment of inertia summed and angular momentum conserved.
concentrated load: A force applied at a single point of a structure, contrasted with a distributed load spread over a length or area.
constraint force: A force from a fixed pivot, hinge, or axle that prevents certain motion, contributing zero torque about the pivot itself but providing real force for translational equilibrium.
contact point: The instantaneous point where a rolling object touches the surface, with zero velocity relative to the ground during rolling without slipping.
control moment gyroscope: A spacecraft attitude-control device that uses motor-driven changes in a gyroscope's axis to rotate the spacecraft through conservation of angular momentum.
coupled equations: A simultaneous set of translational and rotational equations sharing a common variable such as friction force and linked by a constraint equation.
effective inertia coefficient: The factor by which a pulley's mass contributes to the kinetic energy equation after the no-slip substitution, equal to ¼M for a disk and ½M for a ring.
energy distribution ratio: The dimensionless quantity I/(m·r²) that determines the ratio of rotational to translational kinetic energy in a rolling object.
energy partition: The division of total kinetic energy into translational and rotational forms, determined by the moment-of-inertia ratio.
energy partitioning: The division of total mechanical energy among storage modes such as gravitational potential, translational KE, and rotational KE, set by system constraints.
energy redistribution: The process by which friction directs some gravitational potential energy into rotational kinetic energy rather than letting it all become translational.
force asymmetry: A state in which several supports bear different forces because of an asymmetric arrangement of loads.
free body diagram for rotation: A diagram showing all forces on an object with their correct application points, essential for torque analysis since the lever arm depends on where a force acts.
geometric coefficient: The numerical factor in a moment-of-inertia formula that depends only on the shape of the mass distribution, such as ⅖ for a solid sphere.
gravitational torque on gyroscope: The torque τ = Mgr, where M is mass, g is gravitational acceleration, and r is the horizontal distance from pivot to center of mass.
gyroscopic stability: The apparent resistance of a spinning object to changes in its axis direction, because large angular momentum causes torque to produce slow precession rather than tipping.
hollow ring or hoop: A thin ring with all its mass at radius R from the central axis, with moment of inertia I = MR², the maximum possible for given mass and radius.
impulse momentum theorem, rotational: The statement that angular impulse delivered to an object equals its change in angular momentum: τΔt = I(ω_f − ω_i).
instantaneous axis of rotation: The contact point of a rolling object, which acts as a momentary pivot of zero velocity, enabling energy analysis in the stationary frame.
inverse relationship in precession: The precession rate is inversely proportional to the spin rate, because larger angular momentum is harder to reorient with the same torque.
load distribution: The division of total load weight among several supports, determined by the position of the load relative to the supports.
maximum static friction: The upper limit of static friction force, μs·N, beyond which the surfaces begin to slip and kinetic friction acts instead.
moment of inertia ratio: The dimensionless quantity I/(MR²) that determines the fraction of gravitational acceleration available for translation versus rotation.
moment of inertia, i: The rotational analog of mass quantifying how mass is distributed about a rotation axis, computed as I = Σmr² for discrete masses or by integration for continuous bodies.
net torque: The algebraic sum of all individual torques about a chosen pivot, which determines angular acceleration through Στ = Iα.
newton's second law for rotation: The principle that the net torque on an object equals its moment of inertia times its angular acceleration, written Στ = Iα.
no-slip condition: The constraint that a rope wound on a pulley moves at the same speed as the pulley's rim, setting v = ωR and linking translational and rotational variables.
non-uniform object: An object whose mass density varies with position, so its center of mass shifts from the geometric center toward the denser region.
parallel axis theorem: The relation I = I_cm + Md², allowing the moment of inertia about any axis to be found from that about a parallel axis through the center of mass.
point mass: An idealized object with all its mass concentrated at a single point; its moment of inertia at distance r from the axis is I = mr².
precession: The rotation of a spinning object's axis about another axis, caused by a torque perpendicular to the angular momentum vector, changing L's direction but not its magnitude.
precession rate: The angular speed Ω at which the spin axis sweeps around the vertical, equal to τ/L, and Mgr/(Iω) for gravitational precession.
ramp rolling acceleration: The acceleration of an object rolling down an incline, always less than g·sinθ because of the energy cost of rotation.
rifling: Spiral grooves inside a gun barrel that spin a bullet, giving it angular momentum and keeping it pointed forward in flight through gyroscopic stability.
right hand rule for angular momentum: A convention for the direction of the angular momentum vector: curl the right-hand fingers in the rotation direction and the thumb points along L.
rolling constraint: The kinematic relationship between linear and angular motion for rolling without slipping, v = ωR and a = αR, linking translational and rotational dynamics.
rolling without slipping constraint: The kinematic relation a_cm = αR, requiring all rotation to correspond to proportional translation at the contact point without slipping.
rotational dynamics: The study of how torques cause changes in rotational motion, governed by Newton's second law for rotation and the properties of moment of inertia.
rotational equation: Newton's second law applied to rotation, with the sum of torques about the center of mass equal to the moment of inertia times angular acceleration.
rotational inertia: Another name for moment of inertia, emphasizing that it measures an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion.
rotational power: The rate at which work is done on a rotating object, calculated as torque times angular velocity and measured in watts.
rotational work: Energy transferred to or from a rotating system, calculated as torque times angular displacement in radians and measured in joules.
shape dependence: The principle that rolling acceleration depends on the geometric mass distribution rather than total mass or size, since those cancel in the acceleration formula.
shape factor: The ratio of a rolling object's total kinetic energy to ½mv², set by its moment-of-inertia formula and governing the final speed in rolling problems.
sign convention for torque: The standard convention that counterclockwise torque is positive and clockwise torque is negative, enabling algebraic summation of torques.
slipping: A state in which the contact point has nonzero velocity relative to the surface, breaking the rolling constraint and bringing kinetic friction into play.
solid disk moment of inertia: The moment of inertia I = ½MR² for a uniform solid disk rotating about its central axis, reflecting mass averaged at an effective radius less than R.
solid disk or cylinder: A uniform disk or cylinder with mass distributed from center to radius R, with moment of inertia I = ½MR² about its central axis.
solid sphere: A uniform sphere with mass distributed throughout its volume, with moment of inertia I = ⅖MR² about any diameter axis.
static friction in rolling: The friction force at a rolling object's contact point that adjusts to prevent slipping, providing the torque that produces rotation.
steady state precession: Uniform precession at constant angular speed Ω that occurs when both the torque magnitude and the angular momentum magnitude stay constant.
strategic pivot selection: A problem-solving technique of placing the pivot where an unknown or unwanted force acts to eliminate it from the torque equation.
substitution method: An algebraic technique using the rolling constraint to eliminate one unknown so a coupled system can be solved.
thin ring moment of inertia: The moment of inertia I = MR² for a thin ring rotating about its central axis, reflecting that all mass lies at the maximum radius R.
thin rod: A uniform rod with mass distributed along its length L, with moment of inertia I = (1/12)ML² about its center and I = ⅓ML² about one end.
torque as rate of change of l: The fundamental rotational form of Newton's second law, τ_net = dL/dt, valid even when the moment of inertia changes.
torque from friction: The rotational effect of the friction force, equal to f_s·r when computed about the center of mass of a rolling object.
torque versus time graph: A graph in which the area under the curve equals the angular impulse delivered, useful for analyzing situations with changing torque.
translational equation: Newton's second law applied to center-of-mass motion, with the sum of external forces equal to mass times center-of-mass acceleration.
translational equilibrium: The condition in which the vector sum of all forces on an object is zero, preventing any linear acceleration.
translational kinetic energy: The energy associated with the center of mass moving through space, equal to ½·m·v_cm².
vector equation for torque: The equation τ = dL/dt, meaning torque determines the rate of change of the angular momentum vector in both magnitude and direction.
work done by friction: For static friction on a rolling object this work is zero since the contact point has zero displacement; for kinetic friction on sliding it equals −μk·N·d.
amplitude a: The maximum displacement from equilibrium during SHM, always positive and measured in meters, with the object oscillating between +A and −A.
angular frequency: The oscillation rate in radians per second, denoted ω, equal to √(k/m) for a mass on a spring and related to period by ω = 2π/T.
angular frequency omega: The oscillation rate in radians per second; for a spring-mass system ω = √(k/m).
antinode: A point in a standing-wave pattern where the medium oscillates with maximum amplitude due to persistent constructive interference.
base isolation: An earthquake-engineering technique that separates a building from ground motion through flexible bearings, reducing seismic energy transferred to the structure.
blueshift: The decrease in wavelength and corresponding increase in frequency of electromagnetic radiation when the source moves toward the observer.
boundary condition: A constraint that must be satisfied where two media meet, including the requirement that frequency is conserved as wave crests cross the boundary.
bulk modulus: A measure of a material's resistance to uniform compression, equal to the pressure increase needed to cause a proportional volume decrease, related to the speed of sound in a fluid.
closed pipe: A pipe closed at one end and open at the other, producing a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, resonating only at odd harmonics.
coherent sources: Sources emitting waves of the same frequency with a constant phase relationship, required for a stable interference pattern.
compound doppler shift: The combined frequency change when a wave reflects from a moving object, including both the moving-observer effect on receiving and the moving-source effect on re-emission.
compression: A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are displaced toward each other, giving higher than normal density and pressure.
constructive interference: The superposition result when waves arrive in phase at a point, aligning crest with crest so the resultant amplitude equals the sum of the individual amplitudes.
crest conservation: The principle that wave crests cannot be created or destroyed at a boundary, conserving frequency since the crest arrival rate equals the departure rate.
critically damped: The damping regime in which a system returns to equilibrium in the least possible time without oscillating or overshooting.
damping: The gradual loss of mechanical energy in an oscillating system due to nonconservative forces, reducing amplitude over time while the period stays nearly constant.
damping coefficient: A parameter characterizing the strength of the damping force in a system, usually appearing as a constant multiplying velocity in the equation of motion.
destructive interference: The superposition result when waves arrive 180 degrees out of phase, aligning crest with trough so the resultant amplitude equals the difference of the individual amplitudes.
displacement x: The signed distance from the equilibrium point; positive and negative values indicate direction relative to equilibrium rather than distance traveled.
doppler effect: The apparent change in observed frequency when there is relative motion between a wave source and an observer, not a change in the actual emitted frequency.
doppler ultrasound: A medical imaging technique that uses the frequency shift of reflected ultrasound to measure the speed of blood flow or other moving tissue.
driven oscillation: Oscillatory motion that occurs when an external periodic force acts continuously on a system, possibly at a frequency different from the system's natural frequency.
driving frequency: The frequency at which an external periodic force is applied to an oscillating system, which may or may not match the natural frequency.
effective wavelength: The altered spacing between wavefronts in the medium when the source is moving, found by adding or subtracting the distance the source moves in one wave period.
elastic limit: The maximum deformation a spring can undergo while still obeying Hooke's law; beyond this point the force-displacement relationship becomes nonlinear.
encounter rate: The number of wavefronts passing a given point per unit time, equal to the observed frequency and dependent on both wave speed and observer motion.
frequency f: The number of complete oscillations per second, measured in hertz, related to period by f = 1/T.
frequency shift: The difference between observed and emitted frequency, expressed as Δf = f_observed − f_source.
fundamental frequency: The lowest resonant frequency of a system, corresponding to the longest-wavelength standing wave that satisfies the boundary conditions, also called the first harmonic.
gravitational field strength: The gravitational force per unit mass at a location, denoted g, with units of newtons per kilogram or equivalently meters per second squared.
harmonic: A resonant frequency of a system that is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency, corresponding to a shorter-wavelength standing wave that also satisfies the boundary conditions.
in phase: The condition in which two waves reach corresponding points of their cycle, such as crests, at the same time and place.
inverse proportionality: A relationship in which the product of two quantities stays constant, so doubling one halves the other, describing frequency and wavelength at fixed wave speed.
larmor frequency: The natural precession frequency of a nuclear spin in a magnetic field, serving as the resonant frequency exploited in MRI imaging.
linear mass density (μ): The mass per unit length of a string or wire, usually in kilograms per meter, inversely related to wave speed because greater mass per length increases inertia.
linear medium: A medium in which the restoring force on each particle is proportional to displacement, allowing the superposition principle to apply exactly.
longitudinal doppler effect: The frequency shift occurring when source or observer motion has a component along the line joining them, the only Doppler shift classical mechanics predicts for sound.
longitudinal wave: A wave in which particle vibration is parallel to the direction of propagation, characterized by alternating compressions and rarefactions, as with sound in a fluid.
mach number: The ratio of an object's speed to the wave speed in the medium, used to characterize supersonic motion and the onset of shock-wave formation.
maximum acceleration: The greatest magnitude of acceleration during SHM, equal to Aω², occurring at the turning points where displacement is maximum.
maximum speed: The greatest magnitude of velocity during SHM, equal to Aω, occurring as the object passes through the equilibrium point.
mechanical wave: A disturbance that propagates through a medium by particle-to-particle interaction, requiring matter to transfer energy via restoring forces between neighboring particles.
medium transition: The event of a wave crossing a boundary from one material into another, where speed changes with the new medium's properties while frequency stays constant.
natural frequency: The frequency at which a system oscillates freely after being displaced from equilibrium without continuous external driving, determined only by the system's physical properties.
new equilibrium: The position in a vertical spring-mass system where the spring force balances gravity; oscillation occurs about this point and ω is the same as in the horizontal case.
node: A point in a standing-wave pattern where the medium's displacement is always zero due to persistent destructive interference.
odd harmonics: The subset of harmonics whose orders are 1, 3, 5, 7 and so on, the only resonant modes possible in systems with asymmetric boundary conditions such as a closed pipe.
open pipe: A pipe open to the atmosphere at both ends, producing displacement antinodes at both ends and allowing all integer harmonics to resonate.
out of phase: The condition in which two waves reach opposite points of their cycle at the same time and place, in the extreme 180 degrees apart with crest meeting trough.
overdamped: The damping regime in which excessive damping prevents oscillation but the system returns to equilibrium more slowly than critically damped.
parameter: A quantity defining a system's properties, such as mass, spring constant, or length, which can be held fixed or varied to observe its effect on behavior.
path difference: The difference in distance each of two waves travels from its source to a common point, which determines their phase relationship there.
period t: The time taken for one complete oscillation cycle, related to angular frequency by T = 2π/ω.
phase: The position of a particle within its oscillation cycle at a given instant, usually expressed as an angle.
phase constant phi: The angle in radians specifying where in the cycle the object is at t = 0, setting the initial conditions without affecting amplitude or frequency.
phase relationship: The time difference between oscillating quantities; in SHM velocity leads position by π/2 radians and acceleration is π radians out of phase with position.
phase shift: The horizontal displacement of one wave relative to another, measured in time or angle; velocity is shifted 90 degrees ahead of position.
polarization: Restricting transverse wave vibration to a single plane, possible only for transverse waves since longitudinal waves vibrate along just one direction.
potential energy in a spring: The energy stored by elastic deformation, equal to ½kx², where x is the displacement from natural length.
quality factor: A dimensionless parameter describing how underdamped an oscillator is, equal to the ratio of energy stored to energy dissipated per cycle; higher values give sharper resonance peaks.
rarefaction: A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are displaced apart, giving lower than normal density and pressure.
ratio analysis: A problem-solving technique that compares initial and final states as a ratio so unknown constants cancel, isolating the effect of the changed variable.
redshift: The increase in wavelength and corresponding decrease in frequency of electromagnetic radiation when the source moves away from the observer.
refractive index: The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a material, indicating how much light slows on entering and setting the degree of refraction at a boundary.
resonance: The phenomenon in which a driven oscillator reaches maximum amplitude when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, due to phase-locked energy transfer building up over cycles.
resonance curve: A graph showing the amplitude of a driven oscillator as a function of driving frequency, typically peaking at or near the natural frequency.
simple harmonic motion: Oscillatory motion in which the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it, giving sinusoidal position-time behavior.
sinusoidal function: A function with the shape of a sine or cosine wave; in SHM position, velocity, and acceleration are all sinusoids of the same frequency but different phase.
sonic boom: A shock wave produced when a source moves faster than the wave speed, as wavefronts pile up and interfere constructively into a large-amplitude pressure wave.
source frequency: The vibration rate of the object generating a wave, which sets the wave's frequency and remains imprinted on it through any chain of media.
spectral line broadening: The widening of spectral features caused by a distribution of velocities within an extended source, used to measure the rotation rates of stars and galaxies.
spring constant k: A measure of the stiffness of a restoring mechanism, in newtons per meter; a larger k gives a stronger restoring force for the same displacement.
square root scaling: A relationship in which the dependent variable changes by the square root of the factor by which the independent variable changes, characteristic of SHM period dependence.
standing wave: A stationary oscillation pattern formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency traveling in opposite directions, characterized by fixed nodes and antinodes.
steady state: The condition a driven, damped oscillator reaches when the energy input per cycle from the driving force equals the energy dissipated per cycle, giving constant amplitude.
superposition: The principle that when two or more waves overlap in the same medium, the resultant displacement at any point equals the algebraic sum of the individual displacements there.
sympathetic vibration: Vibration induced in one system by resonance with another system oscillating at a matching natural frequency, as between a guitar string and its body.
transverse doppler effect: The relativistic frequency shift observed when a source moves perpendicular to the line of sight, arising from time dilation rather than wavelength compression.
transverse wave: A wave in which particle vibration is perpendicular to the direction of propagation, allowing polarization and typically occurring in media with shear restoring forces.
tuned mass damper: An engineering device of a mass attached to a structure through a spring and damper, designed to oscillate out of phase and absorb energy at resonance.
underdamped: The damping regime in which a system oscillates with exponentially decreasing amplitude, passing through equilibrium several times before eventually stopping.
wave equation: The relation v = fλ expressing the constraint that wave speed equals the product of frequency and wavelength, limiting the possible combinations of these quantities.
wave function: A mathematical expression such as y = A·sin(kx − ωt) describing displacement as a function of both position along the wave and time.
wave number (k): The spatial analog of angular frequency, equal to 2π/λ, giving the radians of phase accumulated per unit distance along the wave.
wave propagation: The process by which a disturbance travels through a medium as each particle's vibration drives the next, creating a moving pattern with no net particle displacement.
wave pulse: A single disturbance traveling through a medium, often used to illustrate superposition when two pulses meet and overlap.
