wave speed (v): The speed at which a wave pattern propagates through a medium, determined by medium properties such as tension and density, not by source frequency or amplitude.
wave speed invariance: The principle that the speed of a mechanical wave depends only on medium properties and not on the motion of the source or observer.
wavefront: A surface connecting all points of a wave that share the same phase, often visualized as a sphere expanding from a point source.
wavelength (λ): The shortest distance between two points of equal phase on a wave, representing the spatial length of one complete cycle.
wavelength compression: The shortening of wavelength when a wave enters a slower medium, needed to keep frequency constant as wave speed decreases.
altitude: The vertical distance above a planet's surface; to find the gravitational field at altitude h, add h to the planet's radius for the total distance from center.
apoapsis: The point in an elliptical orbit farthest from the central body, corresponding to minimum orbital speed and maximum potential energy.
atomic clock: An extremely precise timekeeping device using atomic transitions as a frequency standard, able to detect microsecond discrepancies predicted by relativistic time dilation.
binding energy: The energy required to separate a gravitationally bound system into isolated components infinitely far apart at rest, equal to the magnitude of total mechanical energy.
central body mass: The mass M of the planet or star being orbited, which sets the gravitational field strength and appears in all orbital equations, distinct from the satellite mass.
circular orbit: A closed orbital path in which a satellite maintains a constant distance r from the planet's center, requiring constant orbital speed and continuous centripetal acceleration.
density ratio: The planet's density divided by the satellite's density, determining how far the Roche limit extends; lower satellite density gives a larger Roche limit.
eccentricity e: A dimensionless parameter between 0 and 1 quantifying how elongated an ellipse is; e = 0 is a circle, and values near 1 are highly stretched ellipses.
effective potential: A modified potential energy function used when angular momentum is conserved, including a centrifugal term that creates a barrier preventing orbital collapse to zero radius.
ellipse: A closed curve defined by two foci, where the sum of distances from any point on the curve to the two foci is constant, the shape of all gravitationally bound orbits.
enclosed mass: The total mass contained within a sphere of radius r centered on the mass distribution, which determines the gravitational field at radius r.
energy transfer in orbital changes: The process by which a rocket engine does positive work to move a satellite to a higher orbit, increasing total mechanical energy while decreasing kinetic and raising potential energy.
equal areas in equal times: A geometric consequence of angular momentum conservation stating that the radius vector sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals throughout the orbit.
escape velocity: The minimum initial speed needed for an object to leave a gravitational field without further propulsion, equal to √(2GM/r), derived from zero total mechanical energy.
event horizon: The spherical boundary at the Schwarzschild radius marking the point of no return, where spacetime curvature traps all matter and light inside.
extended object: Any object with finite physical size, so different parts occupy different positions in a gravitational field and experience different gravitational accelerations.
far-side bulge: The tidal bulge on the side of Earth opposite the Moon, formed because Earth's center accelerates toward the Moon faster than the far-side ocean, leaving it behind.
field strength: The magnitude of the gravitational field at a location, equal to G·M/r², with units of N/kg or equivalently m/s².
focus, 복수: foci: One of the two special interior points used to define the shape of an ellipse; in orbital mechanics the large central mass occupies one focus and the other is empty.
geodesic: The straightest possible path through curved spacetime, which an object naturally follows in the absence of nongravitational forces, appearing curved in our three-dimensional perception.
gps time correction: An adjustment applied to GPS satellite clocks for relativistic effects, mainly a 45-microsecond-per-day speedup from weaker gravity at altitude, partly offset by a 7-microsecond slowdown from orbital speed.
gravitational field: A vector field describing the gravitational force per unit mass at every point in the space around a massive object, existing whether or not a test mass is present.
gravitational gradient: The rate at which gravitational acceleration changes with distance from a massive object, arising from gravity's inverse-square dependence on separation.
gravitational lensing: The bending of light paths as light passes through curved spacetime near a massive object, observational confirmation that spacetime curvature affects electromagnetic radiation.
gravitational parameter: The product G·M of a body, often known more precisely than G or M separately; for Earth this value is about 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s².
gravitational potential: A measure of gravitational field strength at a location; lower potential means deeper in the gravity well and produces greater time dilation.
gravitational time dilation: The slowing of the passage of time in a strong gravitational field due to increased spacetime curvature, making clocks near a massive object run slower than distant ones.
gravitational well: A conceptual representation of the gravitational field around a mass, with depth indicating field strength; clocks deeper in the well experience greater time dilation.
gravitationally bound: A state in which an object's total mechanical energy is negative, meaning its kinetic energy is insufficient to escape the gravitational potential energy well.
hohmann transfer orbit: The most fuel-efficient orbital maneuver for transferring between two circular orbits, using an elliptical path tangent to both the initial and final orbits.
hyperbolic trajectory: An unbound path with positive total mechanical energy, resulting in an object escaping to infinity while retaining positive kinetic energy.
inverse square relationship: The mathematical relationship by which gravitational field strength depends on distance, so doubling distance reduces gravity to one quarter.
inverse-square law: The mathematical relationship that gravity decreases in proportion to the square of distance from the source mass, expressed as F = GMm/r².
kepler's third law: The principle that the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius, expressed as T² ∝ r³.
mass to radius ratio: The relationship between a planet's mass and radius that determines surface gravity; large mass packed into a small radius gives strong surface gravity.
neap tide: The reduced tidal range occurring at first and third quarter, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to Earth and their tidal effects partly cancel.
near-side bulge: The tidal bulge on the side of Earth facing the Moon, formed because the ocean there experiences greater gravitational acceleration toward the Moon than Earth's center does.
newton's third law pair: Two equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces acting on two different objects, such as the gravity Earth exerts on you and the gravity you exert on Earth.
orbital decay: The gradual lowering of orbital altitude due to energy loss from drag or radiation, which decreases total mechanical energy yet increases orbital speed.
orbital radius: The distance r from a planet's center to a satellite, equal to the planet's radius plus altitude above the surface, determining both orbital speed and period.
periapsis: The point in an elliptical orbit closest to the central body, corresponding to maximum orbital speed and minimum potential energy.
proper time: The time measured by a clock following a particular path through spacetime, representing the elapsed time actually experienced by an observer on that path.
proportional change: A method of analyzing how a quantity responds when variables in a formula change by known factors; in g = G·M/R², doubling M doubles g and doubling R quarters g.
proportional form: The simplified expression T² ∝ a³ or (T₁/T₂)² = (a₁/a₂)³, useful for comparing orbits around the same central body without knowing G or M.
reference point at infinity: The standard convention in gravitational physics of setting potential energy to zero when two masses are infinitely far apart, establishing a universal baseline.
ring system: A disk of particles orbiting within or near a planet's Roche limit, representing material that tidal forces prevent from coalescing into a moon.
roche limit: The critical orbital distance from a planet within which a satellite held together only by self-gravity is torn apart by tidal forces, about 2.44 × R_planet × (density ratio)^(1/3).
scaling relationships: Mathematical expressions describing how orbital quantities vary with radius: v varies as r^(−1/2), T as r^(3/2), and energies as 1/r.
schwarzschild radius: The critical radius at which the escape velocity from a mass equals the speed of light, calculated as 2GM/c², defining the event horizon size of a non-rotating black hole.
self-gravity: The mutual gravitational attraction between different parts of an extended object, holding it together against external tidal forces that would disperse it.
semi-major axis a: Half the longest diameter of an ellipse, equal to the arithmetic mean of perihelion and aphelion distances, the characteristic size determining the orbital period.
shell theorem: Newton's proof that a uniform spherical shell attracts an external object as if all its mass were at the center and exerts no net force on objects inside it.
singularity: The central point of a black hole where spacetime curvature becomes mathematically infinite and current physical theory cannot describe conditions, distinct from the event horizon.
solid angle: A measure of how large an object appears from a given point, analogous to a two-dimensional angle but extended to three-dimensional geometry.
spacetime: The four-dimensional fabric combining the three spatial dimensions with time, which can curve in the presence of mass and energy, producing the gravitational effects we observe.
spacetime curvature: The bending of spacetime geometry caused by mass and energy, with greater mass producing greater curvature that more strongly affects nearby objects and light.
spaghettification: The extreme vertical stretching and horizontal compression of an object falling into a region of intense gravitational gradient, as near a black hole or neutron star.
spherical shell: A hollow sphere of uniform thickness and density that gravitationally attracts external mass toward its center and exerts no net force on mass inside its empty interior.
spherically symmetric: A mass distribution with the same density at all points equidistant from a central point, for which the shell theorem holds exactly.
spring tide: The increased tidal range occurring at new and full moon, when the Sun and Moon align with Earth and their tidal effects add constructively.
superposition principle: The principle that the total gravitational field at any point equals the vector sum of the individual fields of all masses, requiring component-by-component addition.
symmetry argument: A reasoning method that uses geometric symmetry to identify locations where field components must cancel, without explicit calculation.
test mass: A hypothetical mass small enough that its own gravitational field does not disturb the field being measured, used conceptually to define field strength.
tidal acceleration: The differential gravitational acceleration at a point of an extended object relative to its center of mass, calculated as a_tidal = a_point − a_center.
tidal disruption: The process by which a moon or other object is torn apart when it enters a region, usually inside the Roche limit, where tidal forces exceed its internal gravitational binding.
tidal forces: Differential gravity across an extended object caused by the variation of field strength with distance, capable of stretching an object falling toward a black hole.
tidal period: The time interval between successive high tides at a given location, about 12 hours 25 minutes because Earth rotates under tidal bulges aligned with the orbiting Moon.
tidal scaling law: The mathematical relationship showing that tidal acceleration is proportional to source mass divided by distance cubed (M/r³), derived by differentiating the gravitational acceleration formula.
uniform density: A state in which mass is evenly distributed throughout a volume so the mass per unit volume is the same everywhere; Earth is approximately but not perfectly uniform.
universal gravitational constant g: The proportionality constant in Newton's law of universal gravitation, with value 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², so small that gravity between everyday objects is negligible.
vector field: A field that assigns a vector quantity to every point in space, meaning both magnitude and direction vary with position.
velocity based time dilation: The slowing of time for a moving object predicted by special relativity, causing GPS satellite clocks to lose about 7 microseconds per day due to their orbital speed of about 3.9 km/s.
virial theorem: The relationship that in an equilibrium gravitationally bound system, the time-averaged kinetic energy equals −1/2 the time-averaged potential energy.
vis-viva equation: The formula v² = GM(2/r − 1/a) relating orbital speed to instantaneous distance and semi-major axis, derived from conservation of energy and angular momentum.
zero field point: A location where the vector sum of all gravitational field contributions is zero, requiring the fields of different masses to cancel exactly.
